title: Clay, gold and iron
hookLine: by knowing one lump of clay, the father says, you know everything made of clay: the pot is only a name
last: SOMYA — THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING IS BRAHMAN.

lines: A POT, A CUP, A LAMP, A JAR.
cards: Look along a kitchen shelf in India and there may well be clay on it. A water pot. A cup for chai, thrown away after one use.
A lamp for the evening. A plate, a jar, a tile. Different shapes, different names, different jobs.
Shvetaketu has just asked how there could possibly be one teaching that makes everything known. His father doesn't answer with a theory. He points at the pots.

teach.b: Uddalaka says: my dear, just as by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known, the change is only a name, a matter of words, and the truth is just clay.

In Sanskrit, the end of that line runs: vacarambhanam vikaro namadheyam, mrittiketyeva satyam. Then he says it twice more. By one gold ornament, everything made of gold is known; the truth is just gold.
By one nail-cutter, everything made of iron is known; the truth is just iron. A pot is real. You can carry water in it.

teach.h: THE CHANGE IS ONLY A NAME.
teach.b: But pot is the name for a shape the clay has taken for a while.
Break the pot, and nothing has gone out of existence. The clay is still there; it just doesn't answer to pot anymore.
So if you understand clay, you understand every pot, cup and lamp at once, including ones you'll never see.
Know the clay, and the names stop confusing you.
Over the next lessons, the clay will turn out to be something much bigger: what Uddalaka calls Being, the one stuff under every name. Hindu schools read this line in different ways.
Advaita Vedanta, the school of Shankara, hears the many names as appearance, with only the one ultimately real. Other Vedanta schools, like Ramanuja's, hear the pots as real forms of the one clay.

Both come back to this lump of clay. And you'll hear its echo today. Ask Hindus how one religion can have so many gods, and many will answer with something like this clay: many names and forms, one reality underneath.

how: Vedanta teachers of different schools use Uddalaka's clay, gold and iron as a teaching example, and the clay-and-pot image returns often in later Hindu philosophy.

o: the earth offered into the fire at a ritual
one lump that shows the stuff under every pot
a potter's wheel, a picture of the turning world

games.q: know one, know all — tap the pairs.
p: only a name, a matter of words

s: Uddalaka says the pot doesn't exist
he says the change is a name, a handle of speech, and the truth is the clay.
Uddalaka gives three examples: clay, gold and iron
a lump of clay, a gold ornament, a nail-cutter.
Hindu schools agree on exactly how to read this line
Shankara's Advaita and Ramanuja's school read it differently, as today's lesson says.

games.q: your son asks how one teaching could make everything known. you have a kitchen full of pots. what do you say?
o: it can't; there's too much to know.
know one lump of clay and you know everything made of clay.
memorize the name of every pot.
games.why: Uddalaka answers with clay, then gold, then iron: the change is only a name; the truth is the material underneath.

practice: Hold a cup or a bowl, or just picture one, and say its name in your mind: cup. Then let the name go and notice what's left, the weight, the coolness, the material.
Do the same with your own hand, and rest with whatever is there under the name.

wordCard.voice: The clay. Uddalaka's first example: know one lump of clay, and you know all clay; the pot is a name, a matter of words.

orig.note: Sanskrit mṛttikā: clay, earth. mṛttikety eva satyam: clay alone is the truth.

carryVoice: Keep this: many names, one clay. Tomorrow, what the clay of everything is. See you then.
